findings.description: Battler explains that the expected gag is: he approaches with a lecherous face, she knocks him down and protests. Without that conventional reaction, the joke has no punchline. WH changes 張ッ倒す to ‘Someone trip me’ and お約束 ... オチがつかねぇ to ‘Without your word, I can’t settle down.’ The explanation of his intended comic routine becomes dependence on a verbal assurance and a request to trip him.

「俺がイヤらしい顔で迫る！
張ッ倒す！！
イヤ〜ン、エッチ！
そういうお約束じゃないとオチがつかねぇんだよぉ、頼むよお願いだよ、俺を引っ叩いてくれよ！
こう、バチンっと！
バチンっとぉおぉ〜！！」
contexts.japanesePC: 「…い、今時、こんな献身美徳な子がいるとは…。軽い眩暈すら覚えるぜ。……でも駄目だ！　ダメなんだぁああぁ！！　俺がエロい顔で迫る！　張ッ倒す！！　イヤ～ン、エッチ！　そういうお約束じゃないとオチがつかねぇんだよぉ、頼むよお願いだよ、俺を引っ叩いてくれよ！　こう、バチンっと！　バチンっとぉおぉ～！！」

contexts.WH: "...I-in these days, to think that there's a dedicated and virtuous girl like this...  Getting... giddy again!...  ......But, no!  NooOoo!!  I'm coming at her with a perverted face again!  Someone trip me!!  No~oo, pervert!  Without your word, I can't settle down!  Please, I beg you, smack me!  Like this, smack!  Hit meeee~!!"
contexts.MG:

contexts.UP:
"I come at you with a perverted face!

You gotta complete the joke or it doesn't work! Please, it's a polite request, smack me!
Like this, smack!

contexts.note: Both preserve knocking/smacking Battler down and completing the gag/punchline rather than original WH tripping and verbal-assurance reading.

findings.sourceReading: お約束 denotes the conventional comedy pattern already described in the preceding narration; オチ is the gag’s payoff, and 張っ倒す is knocking someone down with a blow.
findings.alternative: He is desperate for a slap, which both versions preserve later. That does not recover why he asks: the English removes the conventional joke structure rather than merely using a different punchline idiom.

findings.description: Genji dates the exhibition to April of the year before last and says Kinzo had previously ordered the artist to paint it. WH dates the commission itself to that April and then says it was displayed. It collapses the prior commission into the exhibition date.

「あの祖父さまがねぇ。
わざわざ描かせてか…」

contexts.WH: "............You are correct.  In April of the year before last, as it had been arranged, the Master ordered an artist to paint it and it was put on display over there."

contexts.note: Both date exhibition to April of the year before last and explicitly distinguish the earlier commissioning of the painter.

findings.sourceReading: 一昨年の４月に modifies 展示なされた; 兼ねてより ... 描かせていた describes a painting already commissioned and produced.
findings.alternative: ‘As it had been arranged’ could suggest earlier planning, but the English clause still puts ‘the Master ordered an artist to paint it’ inside the April event. Prior commissioning is not retained explicitly.

findings.description: Battler speculates that a parent invented the forest-witch story to keep children safe: perhaps Grandmother, or none other than Grandfather. WH says ‘anybody else other than Grandfather.’ It excludes the very person Japanese explicitly offers as a possible originator.

そう思った親の誰か。
…祖母さまか、あるいは他でもない、祖父さまが言い出したのかもしれない。
さもなくば、はるか大昔からこの島に語り継がれているのか。
contexts.japanesePC: そう思った親の誰か。…祖母さまか、あるいは他でもない、祖父さまが言い出したのかもしれない。

contexts.WH: Someone's parents must have thought so.  ...Maybe my Grandmother, or possibly anybody else other than Grandfather might have said that.

contexts.note: Both explicitly include Grandfather himself as possible originator rather than excluding him.

findings.sourceReading: 他でもない、祖父さま means none other than Grandfather, still under かもしれない.
findings.alternative: The phrase contains 他 and a negation, but they emphatically identify Grandfather rather than exclude him. The later alternative that the story was handed down long ago remains a distinct possibility in both texts.

findings.description: After describing Kinzo’s belief that the witch exists, Jessica ends with a disgusted dismissal: it is creepy or revolting. WH replaces this with ‘I’m sorry, but she just doesn’t exist.’ It removes her emotional reaction and supplies a direct categorical denial in its place.

「……私たちにとっては想像の中の魔女に過ぎないけど、…祖父さまにとっては、彼女はこの島に“い”る存在。
……“い”る。
だから、それを理解することができない私たちにもわかるよう、あの絵を描かせたって言うんだけど」
「………はんッ、気持ち悪いったらありゃしないぜ」
contexts.japanesePC: ………はんッ、気持ち悪いったらありゃしないぜ。」

「………はんッ、気持ち悪いったらありゃしないぜ」
contexts.WH: .........And I'm sorry, but she just doesn't exist."
contexts.MG:
"...She's the witch from Grandfather's delusions.
...Ever since he had this picture hanged, he's been having a harder and harder time telling the difference between truth and fantasy.
...To us, she's just a witch that exists in Grandfather's mind, ...but to him, she's a being that "exists" on this island.
..."Exists".
He says he had that painting made because the rest of us would be incapable of understanding otherwise.
......Hmph, the whole thing's creepy as hell."
contexts.UP:
"......It's the witch from Grandfather's delusions.
...Ever since he had this picture hung up, he's been losing the distinction between fantasy and reality."
"......To us, it's no more than the witch from his imagination, but to Grandfather, she's a being who "exists" on this island.
......‘Exists’.
That's why he says he had that picture painted—so that we'd understand."
".........Hmpf, creeps the hell outta me."
contexts.note: Both preserve Jessica disgust/creepiness rather than replacing it with categorical existence denial.

findings.sourceReading: 気持ち悪いったらありゃしない is emphatic disgust, not a statement of existence or an apology.
findings.alternative: Her preceding claim that this is a witch of imagination already communicates skepticism; a denial is consistent with that stance. The local defect is substituting abstract denial for the particular disgusted outburst, not inventing all of her skepticism or proving a mystery exclusion.

findings.description: Battler remembers Natsuhi seldom joining the children, looking stern and discussing difficult matters with the adults. WH says she gave the impression she was ‘at odds with the other parents,’ changing the content of adult discussion into interpersonal conflict in his childhood memory.

contexts.japanese:
…こう言っちゃ悪いが、嫌いってわけでもないが、特別好きでもない伯母さんだ。
あまり子供の輪に入ってこないし、いつも気難しそうな顔をして、親たちと難しい話をしているという印象しかない。
…実際、あまり言葉を交わしたことがなく、今もどう掴みを取ろうかだいぶ迷ったのだ。
…甲斐なく外してしまったがなー。

…甲斐なく外してしまったがなー。
contexts.WH: She never got into our kids' circle, and she always looked difficult to get along with.  And it didn't help that she gave the impression that she was at odds with the other parents.
contexts.MG:
...It feels bad to say it like this, but while I didn't exactly dislike her, I didn't particularly like her either.
She hardly ever spoke with us kids, and all my memories of her involve her talking to the adults about complicated things, with a scary look on her face.
...In fact, since we hardly ever exchange words, I spent a long time trying to figure out how I should approach her.
...Though my efforts seem to have ended in failure.
contexts.UP:
...It feels bad to say it like this, but—not that I hated her—but I didn't particularly like her.
She never got into our kids' circle, and my only impression of her was as someone who always talked about complicated stuff with my parents while having a crabby expression on her face.
...The fact is, that having barely ever exchanged words, I hesitated a lot even just now about how to approach her.
...Aaand it was pretty much a flop.
contexts.note: Both preserve childhood memory of Natsuhi discussing complicated matters with adults, rather than replacing it with being at odds with parents.

findings.sourceReading: 難しい話をしている is discussing difficult or complicated matters; it does not state she was disagreeing with the people talking.
findings.alternative: The present chapter and earlier scene show genuine adult hostility. That later contextual knowledge does not license replacing the specific earlier memory of difficult discussion with conflict.

findings.description: Kinzo challenges the maxim that knocking opens doors and says the fool who taught it was crucified, then threatens Krauss with the same fate. WH says ‘I’ll crucify the imbecile,’ turning the completed crucifixion reference into another prospective threat. It loses the historical barb while preserving the threat to Krauss.

叩けば扉は開かれると誰が教えた！
その馬鹿者は磔にしたぞッ！！
お前もそうされたいのかッ！！」

お前もそうされたいのかッ！！」
contexts.WH: Who told you the door would open if you knocked!?  I'll crucify the imbecile!!  Do you wish to be as well!!??"
contexts.MG:

I'll crucify the imbecile!!

contexts.UP:

findings.sourceReading: 磔にしたぞ is completed action. The knock-and-open saying also matches the teaching in Matthew 7:7; linking its teacher to crucifixion is an allusion inferred from the juxtaposition, not an independently explicit naming of Jesus in Japanese.
findings.alternative: The first-person threat fits Kinzo’s rage, but the source’s completed tense and the preceding quoted maxim give the clause a different referential function. No literal claim that Kinzo historically crucified Jesus is adopted by the audit.

findings.description: After the water-and-sugar preparation, Genji adds the distinctive flavoring Kinzo likes and adjusts the taste. WH says ‘It improved the original flavor Kinzo liked,’ omitting the separate addition and turning a preparation step into a claim about improvement.

contexts.MG:
......He poured a little into the glass.
Then, he placed a cube of sugar in a strangely shaped spoon and poured water from a pitcher over it.

...It was a strange optical illusion, as though the water had caused a chemical reaction and made the drink become even more unrecognizable as liquor.

...There was no recipe.
Its success was measured only by Kinzo's mood swings when he drank it, and it had taken Genji many decades to learn how to do it right.
contexts.UP:
......He poured a small quantity of the spirit into the glass,
placed a cube of sugar in a strangely shaped spoon, and then poured water from a pitcher over it.
Strangely, when the colorless water was poured into it, the dark green liquid turned a cloudy white.
...It created the strange visual illusion that the water had caused a chemical reaction, which made it all the more difficult to perceive the concoction as liquor.
To this, he added an original flavoring that Kinzo liked, and fine‐tuned the taste.

contexts.note: Both explicitly add Kinzo preferred custom flavoring and then adjust taste, rather than saying it improves the original flavor.

findings.sourceReading: それに ... フレーバーを加え is an addition to the prepared drink; 独自 describes a distinctive or custom flavor, not merely the original flavor being improved.
findings.alternative: ‘Flavor’ could loosely mean taste, but 加え and the sequential recipe specify adding something. No particular ingredient, toxicity or pharmacological effect is identified by the source, so none is inferred.

findings.description: Kinzo explains that Moses drew the sole miracle among an astronomical number of roulette outcomes. WH says he acted ‘instead of betting on incalculable odds’ and found a miracle ‘within the eyes of many.’ The enormous product is misread as an avoided wager, and roulette 目 becomes eyes rather than possible results. The explanation no longer clearly links a singular winning outcome, huge risk and miracle-working luck.

contexts.WH:
That is because Moses, instead of betting on incalculable odds in the roulette of those with power, managed to spectacularly draw to himself the single miracle carved within the eyes of many.  That power that can triumph over astronomical odds!!  Yes, magical power is that fortune through which miracles are grasped!!  To obtain this mighty magic power, one must face the risk of despair!!  Those who possess no magical power call that desperation rather than a bet!
However, people who truly do possess magic power can grasp hold of that miracle and make the enigma come into being!!  And if that power exists within me...!  I'll seize that miracle!  I'll have a chance at making the wish I devoted my life towards come true!!"
contexts.MG:
"Many miracles that happened in myth might be called the crystallization of shocking magic power, with a low probability of occurance and astronomical risk!
That Moses parted the waters of the sea was not a miracle of God—
the risk of that desperate situation, cornered by soldiers on the Red Sea's shores, weighed upon the scales of slaughter and gave birth to that miraculous magic power.
If the same thing occurred again on the same scale, the sea would surely fail to part."
"After all, Moses was able to magnificently summon a miracle engraved on but one of the countless, enumerable results on the roulette of those with power.
That is the force that can triumph over astronomical odds!!
Indeed, good fortune that can grasp miracles is magical power itself!!
To obtain this mighty power, one must face the risk of despair!!
Those who possess no magical power may call that desperation rather than a bet!"
"However, people who truly do possess magic power can grasp hold of that miracle and make the enigma come into being!!
And if that power exists within me...!
I'll seize that miracle! I'll have a chance at making the wish I devoted my life towards come true!!"
contexts.UP:
"All the various miracles that appear in myth can be called crystals of astonishing magic power, obtained through miraculously low probabilities and astronomical risks!"
"That Moses parted the sea was no miracle of God's—
it was that utterly desperate risk, weighed upon the scales of oppression, of being cornered by soldiers on the Red Sea's shores, which gave birth to miraculous magic power!
Even if the same thing occurs again, on the same scope, the sea will no doubt not part."
"That is because Moses managed to spectacularly draw out the single miracle carved in the roulette of those in power, which has more pockets than asougi (10⁵⁶) and nayuta (10⁶⁰) multiplied together."
"The power to triumph over astronomical odds!!
Yes, magical power is, in other words, having the luck to grasp miracles!!
To obtain great magical power, one must bear a risk that is hopelessly great!!
Those who possess no magic would call this not a bet, but pure desperation!"
"However, those who truly do possess magical power can grasp hold of that miracle and make the enigma come into being!!
And if that power exists within me!
I will seize that miracle, I will be able to make the wish I devoted my life towards come true!!"
contexts.note: Both restore roulette outcomes and singular miracle, no eyes phrase or instead-of-betting contradiction. MG numeric specificity separately recorded.

findings.sourceReading: 阿僧祇、那由他を掛けたよりも多く counts an immense number of possible 目; 掛けた belongs to multiplying the large quantities. ひとつだけ刻まれた奇跡 is the sole miracle-result among them.
findings.alternative: The following English lines do preserve defeating astronomical odds and taking great risks, so the whole doctrine is not erased. But ‘instead of betting’ contradicts the illustrative logic, and the eyes phrase fails to express the roulette outcomes that make it intelligible.

findings.description: Battler contrasts lacking energy with being in a bad mood: the former could suggest serious illness, while the latter at least shows Kinzo’s mind or spirit remains firm. WH instead says ‘if he’s not healthy, and his mood is bad’ it proves he is ‘still hanging on.’ This removes the contrast and shifts the immediate inference from mental firmness to continued endurance despite illness.

findings.alternative: ‘Still hanging on’ can imply spirited endurance and partly fit George’s reply. It does not recover the source’s explicit contrast; the English conjunction joins the two states the Japanese separates.

findings.description: Forests, like seas, geographically isolated cultures from one another; they were oceans on land. / Forests were geographically separated from civilization turns a barrier separating cultures into the forest itself being apart from civilization. / Geographically separating one culture from another preserves the barrier function.

contexts.japanese:

文明の光が夜を駆逐するまでの前時代の人類にとって、森は海同様に文化を地理的に隔離する、地上の海同然だったのである。
海に出る漁師たちが、専門的な知識を有してなお命を脅かされることもあるように。
森に出る猟師たちにも専門的な知識が求められ、
同じく命を脅かされることもあったのだ。

contexts.MG:
Nowadays, most people see a forest as a peaceful place,
but to the people of bygone eras, before the light of civilization drove out the night, forests were as geographically separated from civilization as the sea.
They were oceans above the ground.
Fishermen who go out into the ocean are putting their lives at risk, despite their technical knowledge...
In the same way, hunters who go out to the forest are in danger, despite having specialized knowledge of their own.
contexts.UP:
Nowadays, most people see a forest as a peaceful place,
but to the people of bygone eras, before the light of civilization drove out the night, forests were like oceans on land, geographically separating one culture from another.
Just as fishermen who go out into the ocean occasionally have their lives put in danger despite their technical knowledge...
...technical knowledge was also demanded of hunters who went out into the forest,
and their lives were occasionally put in danger just the same.

findings.sourceReading: Forests, like seas, geographically isolated cultures from one another; they were oceans on land.
findings.alternative: Both still depict dangerous wilderness, but the grammatical relation in 文化を地理的に隔離する is cultures being isolated by forests, not forests being isolated from civilization. No separate historical-fact correction or puzzle consequence claimed.

findings.description: Battler interprets the ranking under the misogynist notion that a woman’s womb is borrowed, prioritizing direct children and grandchildren over unrelated spouses. / Womb is something to be borrowed retains the metaphor. / She contributes no genes adds a specific biological proposition absent from the Japanese metaphor.

……気の毒な話だが、その序列によるならば祖母さまが生きていたとして、
その序列は俺よりも下だということになる。
若い日には父に従い、嫁いでからは夫に従い、老いてからは子に従え。
「女、三界に家なし」なんて言われた昔の名残だ。

contexts.MG:
Normally, ranking systems of this sort give spouses equal positions as their partners, but the Ushiromiya family's system was unique.
......Maybe it's a remnant of male chauvinism.
If you start with the assumption that a woman's womb is just something to be borrowed, then the children of direct descent would come first, directly followed by the grandchildren.
In other words, spouses have no blood ties and are therefore placed at the end of the line.
......It's terrible, but by this system, my Grandmother would be ranked even lower than me,
if she were still alive.
In their youth, they obey their father; after they get married, their husband; after aging, their children.
There's the old saying: "Women have no home in any realm".
contexts.UP:
These kind of ranking orders usually permit the spouse a corresponding status, but the Ushiromiya family had an original kind of ranking.
......Maybe it's a leftover of male chauvinism.
Under the notion that a mother's womb is only a temporary house for the child and she contributes no genes, the children of direct descent would have the highest ranking, followed by the grandkids.
Meaning that the spouses, with no blood ties, would be considered the last in line.
......It's terrible, but according to that ranking order, Grandmother, if she was still alive,
would be in a position even lower than mine.
In youth, obey your father; after marriage, your husband; after aging, your children.
A leftover of the times when they used to say, "Women: no home in three worlds".

findings.sourceReading: Battler interprets the ranking under the misogynist notion that a woman’s womb is borrowed, prioritizing direct children and grandchildren over unrelated spouses.
findings.alternative: The added claim explicates an extreme patriarchal view of the mother as a vessel, but the source does not formulate that view as genetic noncontribution. Record the unsupported specificity without treating Battler’s account as author-endorsed biology or inferring a mystery rule.

findings.description: The ornate bottle contains dark green liquid; Genji then pours a little into a glass before adding sugar and water. / In that complex and ornate glass replaces the bottle with a glass before the pouring step. / Complexly designed bottle preserves the initial container.

奇妙な形をしたスプーンに角砂糖を乗せてその上からピッチャーの水を注ぎ込む。

contexts.MG:

......He poured a little into the glass.

Strangely, when the transparent water was poured, the dark green liquid turned a cloudy white.

placed a cube of sugar in a strangely shaped spoon, and then poured water from a pitcher over it.
Strangely, when the colorless water was poured into it, the dark green liquid turned a cloudy white.

findings.sourceReading: The ornate bottle contains dark green liquid; Genji then pours a little into a glass before adding sugar and water.
findings.alternative: Glass could loosely refer to material, but in that ... glass ordinarily names a drinking vessel, especially immediately before poured ... into the glass. The recipe steps otherwise remain operational; no ingredient or poisoning inference established.

findings.description: Kinzo insults Jessica as incompetent and uneducated/unlearned (無能で無学). / Incompetent and uneducated preserves the broad insult. / Incompetent and illiterate substitutes a more specific reading/writing incapacity for lack of education.

findings.description: The sole miracle occupies one outcome among more roulette outcomes than asougi multiplied by nayuta, a named enormous-number product. / Countless, enumerable results omits the named product and its deliberately extravagant scale. / Retains both named numbers and their product.

「その天文学的確率に勝利できる力！！
そう、奇跡を掴み取る運気は即ち魔力なのだ！！
強大な魔力を得るためには絶望的なリスクを背負わねばならぬ！！

contexts.MG:

contexts.UP:

"The power to triumph over astronomical odds!!
Yes, magical power is, in other words, having the luck to grasp miracles!!
To obtain great magical power, one must bear a risk that is hopelessly great!!

findings.sourceReading: The sole miracle occupies one outcome among more roulette outcomes than asougi multiplied by nayuta, a named enormous-number product.
findings.alternative: MG preserves astronomical odds and singular winning outcome, so the main risk/luck argument is restored. This is a limited loss of numeric rhetorical specificity, not recurrence of WH eyes/avoided-bet incoherence or a proven broken puzzle.
